newsitem.title: USA: U.S. 30-year mortgage rates rose in latest week.
newsitem.headline: U.S. 30-year mortgage rates rose in latest week.

text.p: U.S. mortgage rates rose this week on fears of a possible pickup in inflation, Freddie Mac said Thursday.

The average rate on 30-year mortgages rose to 7.54 percent from 7.46 percent last week, while 15-year home loans inched up to 7.07 percent from 7.00 percent, said the agency, which buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for resale to investors.
The average rate on one-year adjustable mortgages also edged higher, to 5.56 percent from 5.53 percent last week.
A year ago, the rate on 30-year loans averaged 7.88 percent, 15-year mortgage rates stood at 7.39 percent and adjustables were 5.81 percent.

"News of a still-growing economy brought on inflation fears this week," Robert Van Order, Freddie Mac chief economist said in a statement. "However, these fears were unfounded, making it unlikely that interest rates will rise further in the week ahead."
In a separate report, the Labor Department said consumer prices rose 0.2 percent in July after reporting Wednesday that producer prices fell 0.1 percent last month.

Federal Reserve policy-makers are to meet Tuesday to consider their next move on interest rates. They last raised short-term rates on March 25, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to ward off inflation. The central bankers have held rates steady since.

Freddie Mac said lenders charged an average of 1.8 percent in fees and points on 30- and 15-year loans, up from 1.7 percent last week. They charged 1.5 percent on adjustable-rate loans, unchanged from last week.
